sections.title: Measuring wrongness
paragraphs: You already know a {{model}} learns from {{input}}-{{target}} pairs. But how does it know when a {{prediction}} is good or bad? It needs a score called {{loss}}.

Think of {{loss}} like a distance between what the {{model}} guessed and what the {{target}} actually was. Bigger gap means worse; smaller gap means better. Zero would mean a perfect match on that example.
For a number prediction, a common choice is squared error: how far off was the guess? For picking one category among many, we use a different formula. The neural network lab will show both.
What matters now is the idea: every training step compares {{prediction}} to {{target}}, computes {{loss}} and asks "how can we do better next time?"
Without {{loss}}, training would be guesswork. With it, the {{model}} has a clear signal for improvement, as long as the {{target}} is trustworthy.
bullets: {{loss}}: a single number summarizing how wrong the {{prediction}} is.
Different tasks: different {{loss}} formulas, same purpose.

check.prompt: A {{model}} predicts 0.9 but the {{target}} is 0.0. What does a high {{loss}} on that row tell you?
check.answer: The prediction is far from the target and should improve
choices: The model is already perfect on that example
The prediction is far from the target and should improve
Loss only applies to image models
High loss means you should delete the training row
check.explanation: {{loss}} measures error. A large gap between {{prediction}} and {{target}} produces high {{loss}}. That is exactly the signal that training should use to nudge {{weights}}.

sections.title: Nudging weights after each mistake
paragraphs: A {{model}}'s behavior is controlled by {{weights}} (and small constants called biases). Training does not rewrite the whole program by hand; it adjusts those numbers.
After computing {{loss}}, the training algorithm figures out which direction each weight should move to reduce error. That direction is the {{gradient}}.
The {{learningRate}} controls step size. A tiny rate makes safe but slow progress; a huge rate can overshoot and make {{loss}} bounce or explode.
One update might look like: read an example → forward pass → compute {{loss}} → adjust {{weights}} slightly along the {{gradient}}. Repeat thousands of times.
This is the loop you will run yourself in the neural network lab. Press Train and watch {{loss}} fall as {{weights}} improve.

reveals.reveal: Fairly high. The {{model}} is under-confident. {{weights}} should move so the next {{prediction}} is closer to 1.0.
Low: almost right. A small {{gradient}} nudge may still help but the error is already small.
{{loss}} jumps wildly because updates overshoot. Turn the rate down and training usually stabilizes.

check.prompt: Training looks stuck: {{loss}} barely moves after many steps. Which knob is the safest first try?
check.explanation: The {{learningRate}} sets update size. Too small crawls; too large oscillates. It is a core {{hyperparameters}} you tune before rewriting the whole {{model}}.

sections.title: Training over many passes
paragraphs: One pass through every training row is one {{epoch}}. A single {{epoch}} is rarely enough for hard puzzles like XOR. The {{model}} needs many chances to refine {{weights}}.
In the lab you will see a {{loss}} chart over time. A healthy training run usually shows {{loss}} trending down, even if it wiggles step to step.
If {{loss}} hits zero on the training rows, the {{model}} may have memorized them. Remember the {{trainSet}} vs {{testSet}} lesson when you interpret results.

The neural network lab lets you change hidden size, activation, dataset and {{learningRate}}. Your goal is not magic numbers; it is to connect "I changed a setting" to "{{loss}} and {{prediction}}s changed."
Try the optional **Loss and updates lab** from this lesson to watch {{loss}} fall as you train. Then open the **Neural network lab** for full controls on XOR and more datasets.
bullets: {{epoch}}: one full sweep through the training data.
Watch {{loss}}: your main feedback while training.
Then try the lab: connect formulas to a network you control.

check.prompt: In one short phrase: what is training trying to do to {{loss}}?
check.explanation: Training adjusts {{weights}} to push {{loss}} down so {{prediction}}s match {{target}}s. That is the entire point of the update loop you are about to run in the lab.

recapQuestions.prompt: Why must a {{model}} compute {{loss}} during training?
recapQuestions.answer: To know how wrong predictions are and how to update weights
choices: To know how wrong predictions are and how to update weights
To replace the need for targets
To avoid using a train set
To make predictions random on purpose
recapQuestions.explanation: {{loss}} compares {{prediction}} to {{target}} and drives {{gradient}} updates. Without it, the {{model}} would not know which direction to adjust {{weights}}.

recapQuestions.prompt: You run 50 {{epoch}}s and training {{loss}} is still flat. Which pair of ideas from this lesson matter most?
recapQuestions.answer: Learning rate and whether loss can improve on this data
choices: Delete labels and hope for the best
Learning rate and whether loss can improve on this data
Only measure loss on the test set while training
recapQuestions.explanation: Flat {{loss}} often means updates are too small ({{learningRate}}) or the {{model}} lacks capacity for the task. You still need a training signal. Never drop {{target}}s or leak the {{testSet}} into tuning.
